aka: Ajinomoto Build-up Film, build-up film, ABF build-up film, ABF substrate, ABF substrates
plain: The insulating film inside the base board, the substrate, that a high-end chip package sits on. The board is built up in layers, and a sheet of this epoxy film, about 10 micrometers thick, separates each layer of copper wiring from the next. The Japanese food company Ajinomoto first developed it in 1999.
why: Ajinomoto told investors in June 2026 that its film has held a share of over 95 percent since its launch, and it says practically all high-performance computers and servers rely on it.

aka: AI accelerator, XPU, accelerators
plain: A chip built to do the one kind of arithmetic machine learning needs, multiplying large grids of numbers, far faster than a general-purpose processor can. Nvidia's graphics processors, Google's Tensor Processing Units and Amazon's Trainium are all accelerators.
why: Accelerators are what the whole supply chain is for, and the unit that export licenses are granted or refused for.

aka: 2.5D packaging, 3D packaging, 2.5D, 2.5D work, advanced packaging plants
plain: The steps that assemble several finished chips into one component, sitting side by side or stacked, wired together closely enough to behave like a single larger chip. Ordinary packaging only puts one chip into a protective case with contacts on the bottom.
why: A modern AI accelerator needs more circuit than one exposure can print, and its memory must sit beside the logic, so it is assembled this way. Epoch AI found that TSMC's CoWoS packaging and the memory itself were the main limits on AI chip production in 2025.

aka: atomic layer deposition
plain: A way of coating a chip roughly one atomic layer at a time. Each pulse of gas sticks to the surface and then stops once the surface is covered, so the film ends up the same thickness on the floor and on the walls of a hole more than 50 times deeper than it is wide.
why: US regulators call atomic layer deposition an enabler of stacked memory and of FinFET and gate-all-around logic, and export rules name some of its tools directly. Chinese toolmakers held 2.6 percent of the market in 2025 on CSET's count, most of it from Piotech.

aka: application-specific integrated circuit, custom silicon, ASICs, custom accelerator, custom accelerators, custom chip, custom AI silicon, custom AI ASICs
plain: A chip designed for one company's own workload and not sold on the open market. Google's Tensor Processing Unit and Amazon's Trainium are chips of this kind; an Nvidia part sold to any customer is not.
why: A custom chip is tuned to one company's workload, while a chip sold to everyone comes with mature software and a resale market. Design houses such as Broadcom and Marvell turn the buyer's design into silicon and sell it the finished chips.

aka: automated test equipment, tester
plain: The machine that connects to a finished chip, feeds it millions of test patterns and checks whether the answers coming back are right. Advantest counts test as the only manufacturing step that puts electricity through the chip.
why: An AI accelerator joins a dozen expensive pieces, and one bad piece scraps them all, so each die is tested first. Advantest's April 2025 investor guide put Advantest and Teradyne at about 80 percent of the tester market.

aka: ball grid array, FC-BGA, flip-chip BGA
plain: A way of joining a packaged chip to a circuit board using a grid of small solder balls across the underside in place of a row of pins around the edge. Heating the assembly melts every ball at once into a permanent joint.
why: The number and spacing of those balls limit how much current and how many signals can reach a package.

aka: BOM
plain: The itemized list of every purchased part in a finished product and what each part cost, the way a builder's invoice prices lumber, wiring and fixtures separately.
why: Epoch AI estimated in December 2025 that memory made up about half of the roughly $6,400 manufacturing cost of an Nvidia B200, so the bill of materials shows which suppliers capture the money a buyer spends.

aka: Bureau of Industry and Security, part of the US Department of Commerce
plain: The US government office that decides which technologies may be exported, to whom, and on what conditions. It writes the rules, issues the licenses and brings the enforcement cases.
why: Washington built its restrictions on selling AI chips and chipmaking tools to China one bureau rule at a time, and the bureau can change a threshold with a Federal Register notice, with no act of Congress needed.

aka: capital expenditure, capital spending
plain: Money a company spends on long-lived physical assets such as buildings, machines and servers, as distinct from salaries and other running costs.
why: It buys the chips, racks and buildings, so the largest cloud companies' capex pays for the AI buildout. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle spent $448.2 billion of capital in 2025, and Epoch AI says they will spend $770 billion in 2026 if that trend continues.

aka: chiplets
plain: One of several smaller pieces that a chip has been deliberately split into, each manufactured separately and then wired back together inside a single package. A chip built this way is a house assembled from prefabricated rooms.
why: Many large accelerators need more circuit than one exposure can print, so they are built from chiplets. That moves the hard part into packaging, and Epoch AI found that TSMC's CoWoS packaging and memory were the main limits on AI chip production in 2025.

aka: chokepoints
plain: A step in the supply chain where so few firms or countries can do the work that losing one of them stops everybody.
why: Chokepoints are where a policy has effect, and where one sanction or one factory fire reaches the whole industry.

aka: training compute threshold
plain: A limit set on the amount of arithmetic used to train an AI model. It counts operations, whichever chips run them. The AI Diffusion rule of January 2025 made one an export control. ECCN 4E091 covers "'Parameters' for an artificial intelligence model trained utilizing 10^26 or more 'operations'", and 15 CFR 742.6(a)(13) requires a license for them to every destination worldwide. Article 51(2) of the EU AI Act draws Europe's line ten times lower, presuming high-impact capabilities when the cumulative computation used for training is "greater than 10^25" floating point operations.
why: Every other control threshold measures a chip, and this one measures the model the chips train. The US and EU numbers differ by a factor of ten, and Article 51(3) lets the European Commission move its figure by delegated act. BIS said in May 2025 that it would not enforce the AI Diffusion rule, but 4E091 still stands in the regulations.

aka: concentration band
plain: A four-band judgment of how many firms could credibly supply a stage today, taken at the narrowest step inside it. Extreme means three or fewer, or one firm holding more than half the stage. High means four to six, with the top two taking most of the revenue. Moderate means seven or more, none of them dominant. Low means many, with the scarce input something another industry sells at volume. Where a figure exists for the top country's share of the segment, it serves as a second check, and the supplier count wins when the two disagree.
why: The fewer the firms that can do a stage, the more one accident or one license decision moves the whole chain.

aka: Country Group, Country Group D:5, D:5, A:5, D:1, D:3, D:4, arms-embargoed countries
plain: The groups that US export rules sort the world's countries into, published as supplement no. 1 to 15 CFR part 740. A:5 and A:6 are close partners; D:1, D:4 and D:5 are the national security, missile technology and arms-embargoed groups; E:1 and E:2 are the most restricted. A country can sit in several at once, and the license requirement usually turns on which.
why: License rules for AI chips are written in country groups. Chips in the 3A090.b band need a license for D:1, D:4 and D:5 destinations not also in A:5 or A:6, and for the UAE, which moved from D:3 and D:4 into A:5 in July 2026 and is named in the rule, with approved Emirati consignees exempted (15 CFR 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(B)).

aka: chip on wafer on substrate
plain: TSMC's method for mounting logic chips and memory stacks side by side on a shared interposer, a layer of fine wiring, then mounting that interposer on a rigid base board. In CoWoS-S the interposer is one piece of silicon; in CoWoS-L, which carries Blackwell and Rubin, it is redistribution wiring with small embedded silicon bridges. Nearly every high-end AI accelerator is built this way.
why: TSMC's CoWoS packaging and memory were the main limits on AI chip production in 2025, and Epoch AI puts Nvidia at 60.3 percent of all CoWoS that year. SemiAnalysis judged in March 2026 that CoWoS supply was easing, but in July 2026 TSMC said its packaging capacity was so tight that it limited customers' growth.

plain: The share of controlled American content a foreign-made item may contain before US export rules, the EAR, apply to it. Under 15 CFR 734.4 the general threshold is 25 percent of the item's value, and 10 percent for the most restricted destinations. Above the line the item is caught; below it, it is not.
why: It decides whether foreign-made goods with some US content fall under American rules. The foreign direct product rules work differently and catch an item whatever its share of US content. 15 CFR 734.4(a)(3) sets no de minimis level for the equipment in ECCN 3B993.f.1 when it is bound for advanced-node chip production, unless the country it was first exported from also controls it.

aka: D0, defects per square centimeter
plain: The average number of chip-killing flaws per square centimeter of processed wafer. It is a fab's quality score, inferred from how many chips come out working.
why: AI accelerators have the largest dies in production, and yield falls steeply with die area times defect density. On an 8 square centimeter die, halving defect density lifts the share of flawless dies from about 49 to about 69 percent. The share that can be sold is higher on chips that carry spare blocks.

plain: An order from BIS that shuts a named party out of trade in US-controlled items, as a sanction or a protective measure, with no license policy involved. Under 15 CFR 764.3 it restricts the party's exports, reexports and in-country transfers of items subject to the EAR, and its access to them, and it can suspend or revoke the party's outstanding licenses. There is no application to file. Orders can be issued outright or suspended and later activated.
why: It can cut a named party off from every item subject to the EAR. The order activated against ZTE in April 2018 stayed in force until BIS terminated it 89 days later on settlement (83 FR 17644; 83 FR 34825).

plain: Adding a layer of material to a wafer, either by knocking atoms off a solid target so they land on the surface, or by reacting gases at the surface so a film grows there. It is how the insulators, the wires and the parts of each transistor are built up.
why: Making a chip often takes more than a thousand steps, many of them deposition and etch, and AI hardware needs films that reach the bottom of deeper holes. Four firms make most of the tools, and deposition is among the tool types where Chinese makers gained the most share between 2019 and 2024.

aka: singular of dice, dies
plain: One rectangular chip cut out of a wafer. Hundreds are printed side by side on the same disc and then sliced apart, and each separated rectangle is a die.
why: Cost and yield are counted per die, and a GPU die that fills a whole printed field loses far more silicon to one fatal defect than a small chip does.

aka: dynamic random-access memory
plain: A computer's main working memory. Each bit is a charge held in a microscopic capacitor that leaks, so the chip has to refresh its contents constantly, and it forgets everything when the power goes off.
why: HBM is a stack of DRAM chips, and the three leading DRAM makers, SK hynix, Samsung and Micron, make nearly all of it. SK hynix says the shift of production capacity to HBM left ordinary DRAM, the kind in PCs and phones, undersupplied and helped drive a significant price recovery from the third quarter of 2025.

aka: deep ultraviolet, deep-ultraviolet, DUV scanner, DUV scanners, DUV tools
plain: The older kind of chipmaking light, and the machines that print with it, which still make up most lithography tools. The light comes from gas lasers, at 248 or 193 nanometers. Filling the gap between lens and wafer with water sharpens the image, a method called immersion.
why: Without extreme ultraviolet, a fab reaches leading-edge logic only with immersion deep ultraviolet and several passes per layer, as SMIC does, so immersion is where Dutch export licensing draws its line.

aka: Export Administration Regulations
plain: The body of US rules that governs the export of commercial goods, software and technology, including items with both civilian and military uses, written and enforced by the Bureau of Industry and Security. They run from 15 CFR part 730 to part 774: part 734 sets what they cover, part 742 the license requirements, part 744 the end-use and end-user controls, part 740 the exceptions and part 764 the penalties.
why: American export rules on chips and chipmaking tools are amendments to these regulations, made by notice in the Federal Register with no act of Congress.

plain: The label for an item that falls under US export rules but is not named on the Commerce Control List, the catalog of controlled items, from 15 CFR 734.3(c). It is a residual category with conditions: an EAR99 item still needs a license if it is going to a listed party or a controlled end use.
why: An EAR99 item can usually ship without a license, but a listed buyer, a controlled end use or an embargoed destination can still require one, which is why the end-user controls in part 744 matter to exporters of unlisted items.

aka: Export Control Classification Number
plain: The catalog number that US export rules assign to a controlled item, rather like a customs tariff code for security-sensitive technology. Number 3A090 covers advanced computing chips and 3B001 covers chipmaking equipment.
why: An item's classification number decides whether it needs a license, so the technical thresholds written into each number are where the policy takes effect.

aka: electronic design automation, chip design software
plain: The software that turns a description of what a chip should do into the exact pattern of shapes to be printed on silicon, and proves the result will work before anyone commits money to masks and wafers.
why: Three vendors sell the only complete design flows used at the leading edge. Since October 2022 software made for designing chips with gate-all-around transistors has needed a US export license, and in May 2025 the US government required a license for all their sales to China with letters to the vendors, until it lifted the requirement on 2 July.

aka: end user, end users, end-user, end use, military end user
plain: Export rules that turn on who the buyer is and what they will do with the item, whatever the item is. The same tool can ship freely to one customer and need a license that will be refused for another.
why: These controls reach past the product to the customer, so a company can lose access because of who owns it or what its site produces, as when US rules were extended in September 2025 to firms at least 50 percent owned by listed entities, an extension now stayed to 9 November 2026.

aka: entity-list, Entity-Listed, Entity List additions, listed entity, listed entities, listed firm, listed firms
plain: A published list of foreign companies, institutes and individuals that need a license before anyone anywhere, American or foreign, may send them an item subject to the EAR. Each entry states its own license review policy, so a listing is not one uniform outcome: most carry a presumption of denial, meaning the license will normally be refused. SMIC's, as amended in December 2024, is a presumption of denial for all items, except that tools designed for 200 mm wafer production and bound for a 200 mm plant are read case by case. It is supplement no. 4 to 15 CFR part 744, and the license requirement is in 15 CFR 744.11.
why: It names an organization, so it is one of the simplest instruments Washington has. Since September 2025 a listing has reached companies at least 50 percent owned by listed firms, though that extension is stayed to 9 November 2026 (90 FR 50857).

aka: etching, etched, etches, etcher, etchers, dry etch
plain: Removing material from a wafer wherever the printed pattern says it should not be, usually by turning a gas into a plasma whose ions and fragments eat one material while leaving the material beside it alone.
why: Wrap-around transistors need etch that cuts sideways while sparing the material beside it, and stacked memory needs holes far deeper than they are wide, so US rules control etch tools by selectivity and hole shape.

aka: extreme ultraviolet, extreme-ultraviolet, EUV scanner, EUV scanners, extreme ultraviolet lithography
plain: The light that prints the finest layers of every leading-edge chip, and the machines that print with it. Its wavelength is 13.5 nanometers, and shorter light draws finer lines. Air and glass both absorb it, so the machine works in a vacuum and carries the light on mirrors. The light comes from droplets of molten tin, 50,000 a second, each hit twice by a laser.
why: The finest layers set how densely transistors and wires pack, so the most advanced AI chips depend on EUV. Only ASML makes the machines, and export controls block it from shipping them to Chinese chipmakers.

aka: fabrication plant, wafer fab, fabs, chip factory, chip factories
plain: The factory where wafers are processed into chips. It is a cleanroom where each wafer moves between hundreds of machines in a sealed pod for months, and the building costs tens of billions of dollars.
why: In 2023 BCG estimated that a new 2 nm-class fab finished in 2026 would cost $35 to $43 billion to own over ten years. Money can buy the building faster than it can train a workforce, and TSMC has yet to build one of its largest fabs outside Taiwan.

plain: A chip company that designs and sells chips but owns no factory, paying a contract manufacturer, a foundry, to make them. Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm and Broadcom all work this way.
why: The fabless model concentrates manufacturing in a handful of foundries, so a designer's supply, cost and geographic exposure are set by a company it does not control.

aka: fin field-effect transistor
plain: A transistor whose channel, the strip that current flows through, is stood on edge like a shark fin, so that the gate, the electrode that switches the current, wraps around three of its sides instead of resting on one. More contact means firmer control and less leakage when the switch is meant to be off.
why: TSMC built its processes on FinFETs until N2, its first nanosheet node, entered volume production in late 2025. The October 2022 US rules used FinFET or 16/14 nm logic as one of their thresholds for an advanced fab.

aka: floating point operations per second, TFLOPS, PFLOPS, FLOP, teraflops
plain: A count of how many arithmetic operations on floating-point numbers, numbers with a fractional part, a chip can perform each second, the way horsepower counts an engine's output.
why: It is the standard unit of AI compute, but a figure compares across chips only when the number format behind it is stated. US export rules use their own score, TPP, which weights each operation by its bit length.

aka: FDPR, FDP rule, foreign-produced direct product rule, direct product rule, foreign-produced item rules, foreign-produced item rule, foreign-produced item
plain: A US rule that puts a foreign-made item under American control when two tests are both met. The first is about the product: the item was made directly from specified US technology or software, or in a plant that was. The second is about the destination: the item is going somewhere, or to someone, the rule names. Both halves are needed. The mechanics are in 15 CFR 734.9.
why: The rule is what makes US controls extraterritorial. Without it a listed buyer could order the same chip from a supplier outside America; with it, a chip made in Taiwan on American tools for a listed Chinese firm needs a US license.

aka: pure-play foundry, contract chipmaker, foundries, pure-play, pure play, pure-play model, contract chipmaking
plain: A factory business that manufactures chips designed by other companies and makes only its customers' products. TSMC, founded in 1987, pioneered the model, and it works because no chip company sells enough of one product to fill a modern fab on its own.
why: All six of TSMC's largest plants are in Taiwan, which makes over 70 percent of the world's chips below 10 nm, so one island's politics reaches the whole chip supply.

aka: 8-bit and 4-bit floating point, FP8, FP4, FP16, BF16, INT8, number formats
plain: Ways of writing a number using only 8 or 4 binary digits, or bits, far fewer than standard formats use. Each number is less precise, but the chip can perform and store far more of them, which suits machine learning better than it would suit accounting.
why: Lower precision raises a chip's headline speed, so a performance figure quoted without its number format cannot be compared, and US export rules weight each operation by its bit length.

aka: GAA, nanosheet transistor, RibbonFET at Intel, nanosheet, nanosheets, RibbonFET, GAA transistor, gate-all-around transistors
plain: A transistor in which the gate, the electrode that switches the current, wraps all the way round the channel that current flows through; a fin's gate touches three sides. Surrounding the channel gives the gate full control, so the switch still turns fully off as dimensions shrink.
why: Only TSMC, Intel and Samsung can build it. It needs etch that cuts sideways, which US export rules control, and customers building 2 nm gate-all-around capacity lifted ASM International, the leader in atomic layer deposition, to record revenue in 2025.

aka: graphics processing unit, GPUs
plain: A processor originally built to draw video game images by doing thousands of simple calculations simultaneously. That same shape of arithmetic turned out to be what neural networks need, so this chip became the default AI processor.
why: Nvidia used 60.3 percent of all CoWoS packaging in 2025 on Epoch AI's estimate, and its GPUs, such as the H20 and H200, are the chips at the center of recent US license decisions.

plain: The share of a sale left over after paying what it cost to make the thing, before research, sales and overheads are counted. A 70 percent gross margin means $70 of every $100 of revenue survives manufacturing cost.
why: Gross margin shows where pricing power sits. In quarters ending June to September 2026, Micron's was 86.8 percent, Nvidia's 75.0 percent and KLA's 61.4 percent, against 36.4 percent at the substrate maker Ibiden and 16.8 to 27.3 percent at the assembly and test houses Amkor and ASE, counting ASE's packaging and test segment alone.

aka: high bandwidth memory, high-bandwidth memory, HBM3E, HBM4, HBM4E, HBM stack, HBM stacks, memory stacks, stacked memory
plain: Stacked memory built for AI chips. Up to sixteen memory chips are stacked into a cube and wired together through copper-filled holes made in each chip before stacking, and the cube sits a few millimeters from the processor. It holds the model the chip is running, the numbers called weights, and hands them to the processor over 1,024 or more wires at once.
why: To write each word of an answer, the chip reads the whole model from this memory, along with the record of the conversation so far. A larger model or a longer conversation needs more memory, so the size and speed of HBM usually set how many people one chip can serve. It is the largest line in the bill of materials of an Nvidia B200, and SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make nearly all of it.

aka: high numerical aperture extreme ultraviolet, ASML EXE series, High-NA, High NA, High-NA scanners, High-NA machine, High-NA tools
plain: The next generation of extreme ultraviolet machine, whose larger mirrors collect light over a wider angle and so print smaller features. The wider optics also halve the area the machine can print in one exposure, so a large chip has to be stitched together from two exposures.
why: It cuts the smallest printable feature from 13 nanometers to 8, and TSMC expects more AI chip layers to need it. Each machine sells for an estimated $350 to $400 million. Intel says it uses it in volume production for select layers of some 18A products, and TSMC plans to use it in high-volume manufacturing from 2030.

aka: direct bond interconnect, SoIC, Foveros, copper pad to copper pad
plain: Joining two chips face to face by pressing their copper pads, and the glass-like insulator around them, into direct contact, with no solder in between. Removing the solder lets connections be packed much more tightly and shortens the path heat has to travel out.
why: It would cut the spacing between connections in a memory stack from about 20 micrometers to under 1, and an SK hynix tech note expects full-scale use in HBM at HBM4E or HBM5, where stacks are projected to pass twenty layers.

aka: hyperscalers
plain: One of the handful of companies that run data centers at global scale, such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta and Oracle.
why: They pay for the AI buildout. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle spent $448.2 billion of capital in 2025.

aka: integrated device manufacturer, integrated device maker, integrated device makers
plain: A chip company that both designs its products and manufactures them in its own factories. Intel, Samsung and Micron are examples.
why: An integrated maker that also rents out factory capacity competes with its own customers, and its own products take the best capacity, so fewer customers trust it with a flagship design.

aka: transfer (in-country)
plain: A change in the end use or the end user of an item inside one foreign country, defined at 15 CFR 734.16. Nothing crosses a border: a server legally imported into a country for one customer is transferred when it is resold, or repurposed, for another.
why: It is the step that catches hardware diverted after it has landed, and it is why a license granted for a named Chinese customer does not travel with the hardware. Reexports and in-country transfers of advanced chips to Macau or Country Group D:5 keep a presumption of denial even where an export from the United States would be read case by case (91 FR 1684).

aka: interposers, silicon interposer, silicon carrier
plain: A layer of wiring with no transistors, used as a miniature circuit board underneath several chips so they can be connected at a density no ordinary board could reach. It is either one piece of silicon or layers of fine copper wiring with small silicon bridges.
why: HBM connects over 1,024 or 2,048 wires, too many for a resin board, so memory and logic sit together on an interposer. Its area caps how much fits in one package, now 5.5 times the reticle on TSMC's CoWoS-L.

aka: is informed letter, is-informed letters, by letter
plain: A letter from BIS to one named company imposing a license requirement on a specific export, without any rule being published. The authority is written into the regulations themselves, for example 15 CFR 744.23(b), which lets BIS inform a person individually, with no amendment to the EAR.
why: It imposes a control at once, with no published rule. The April 2025 license requirement for Nvidia's H20 arrived this way, and the public learned of it from Nvidia's own filing.

aka: KGD, good die, good dies, known good die
plain: A bare chip tested thoroughly enough, before assembly, to be trusted inside something expensive. In an ordinary product a faulty chip wastes one chip; inside a package that joins a dozen expensive pieces, one bad die throws away all of them.
why: As packages grow toward about ten large compute dies and 20 memory stacks, the cost of catching a bad die late pushes testing and burn-in, running chips hot to force early failures, back onto the wafer.

aka: license exception
plain: A written carve-out in export rules that lets a shipment go without an individual license, if it meets stated conditions. The ones that matter for AI chips and chipmaking tools are NAC and ACA (15 CFR 740.8), HBM (740.25), AIA and LPP, which carry the top band of accelerators to allies and in small volumes elsewhere (740.27 and 740.29), IEC for countries that adopt matching controls (740.24), and RPL for servicing and spare parts (740.10).
why: Exceptions are how a control regime is tuned without rewriting it, and how Washington rewards allies. License Exception IEC, added in September 2024, covers exports to and by countries that have put equivalent controls in place (89 FR 72926).

aka: ACA, Advanced Computing Authorized
plain: An export rule that lets AI chips below the top band ship to most of the world with no license and no advance notice. It covers the same chips as its companion exception NAC, and every destination except Macau, Country Group D:5 and firms headquartered in either. The top-band data center chips in ECCN 3A090.a are excluded and need a license to any destination. BIS split it from NAC at 15 CFR 740.8 in April 2024, and the AI Diffusion rule widened it in January 2025 to the whole world outside Macau and D:5.
why: It lets chips below the top band reach most of the world with no license or advance notice, while NAC keeps a notice requirement for Macau and D:5. Before April 2024 NAC did both jobs, so an older table that shows one exception describes what is now two.

plain: An export rule that lets high bandwidth memory go to a packaging site with no license, to be packaged beside a chip, if its memory bandwidth density is below 3.3 GB/s per square millimeter, measured over the area of the package or stack. The exporter must be headquartered in the United States or Country Group A:5, memory bound for Macau or Country Group D:5 must be bought by the chip's designer, and the stacks must go straight to the packaging site. It does not cover packaging at a facility in Macau or D:5 that also makes advanced-node chips. It sits at 15 CFR 740.25.
why: It keeps Chinese packaging houses in the supply chain of American and allied chip designers, while a sale of the same stacks to a Chinese buyer still needs a license. HBM needs a license only for Macau and Country Group D:5, and the exception was written into the December 2024 rule that first controlled HBM (89 FR 96790).

aka: LPP, Low Processing Performance
plain: An export rule that lets a buyer almost anywhere receive a capped amount of top-band AI chips each year without a license. The cap is 26,900,000 TPP, the export rules' measure of computing power, per ultimate consignee per calendar year. Macau, Country Group D:5 and firms headquartered in either are excluded, and it does not cover transfers within a country. The AI Diffusion rule created it in January 2025, at 15 CFR 740.29.
why: It lets buyers outside the nineteen destinations in supplement no. 5 to part 740 take top AI chips in small amounts with no license application. BIS said in May 2025 that it would not enforce the AI Diffusion rule, but it withdrew none of the text, so LPP still stands in the regulations beside AIA, ACM and the nineteen-destination list.

aka: NAC, Notified Advanced Computing
plain: An export rule that lets AI chips below the top band ship to Macau and Country Group D:5, and to firms headquartered there, with no license, if the exporter notifies BIS at least 25 calendar days ahead and BIS does not say a license is needed. The top-band data center chips in ECCN 3A090.a and the memory in 3A090.c are excluded. It sits at 15 CFR 740.8.
why: It lets these chips reach the restricted destinations without a license application. Since April 2024 the section has carried two exceptions, NAC for the restricted destinations and ACA for everywhere else.

aka: direct-to-chip cooling, cold plate cooling, cold plate, cold plates, liquid-cooled, direct-to-chip liquid, direct liquid cooling
plain: Taking heat out of a processor by pumping liquid through a cold plate on the chip package, instead of blowing air across a finned heatsink. A building loop then carries the heat outdoors.
why: Nvidia's GB300 NVL72 rack is liquid cooled and its Rubin platform entirely so, and Nvidia says every cloud provider and data center operator building for Rubin is moving to liquid.

aka: photolithography
plain: Printing a circuit pattern onto a wafer by shining light through a patterned plate and projecting a shrunken image of it onto a light-sensitive coating. It is photography at the scale of nanometers, repeated once for every layer of the chip.
why: It is the most concentrated stage in the chain, and the finest layers it prints set how densely transistors and wires pack.

plain: The widening gap between how fast a processor can calculate and how fast memory can feed it numbers to work on. Arithmetic has grown cheap faster than moving numbers has.
why: An AI chip reads its whole model from memory for each word it writes, so memory size and speed usually set how many people one chip can serve. Memory is also about half the cost of building an Nvidia B200, on Epoch AI's estimate.

aka: process control, when grouped with inspection, metrology and inspection, inspection tools
plain: Measuring what a factory actually built: how wide a printed line came out, how thick a film is, whether this layer sits exactly on top of the last one. Inspection is the related job of finding flaws.
why: A fab that cannot buy sensitive inspection tools finds fewer of the defects that lower its yield, so its yield rises more slowly. KLA held 56.8 percent of the market for these tools in 2025, by CSET's count.

aka: double patterning, quadruple patterning, self-aligned quadruple patterning, multiple patterning, multi-patterning, several passes, several exposures, multiply exposed, DUV multipatterning
plain: Printing a single chip layer using two, three or four separate plates and etching steps, because one exposure cannot resolve features that close together. It is what a fab does when it cannot get sharper light.
why: SMIC reaches its most advanced processes without extreme ultraviolet machines by printing its tightest layers in several passes on deep ultraviolet tools. Each extra pass costs a mask, machine time and a chance to misalign.

aka: process node, technology node, for example N2 or 18A, nodes
plain: The name a foundry gives one generation of its manufacturing process. The number in the name no longer measures anything on the chip, and SMIC's N+3, a 7 nm-class process, spaces its narrowest wires closer together than Intel's 18A does.
why: Node names measure nothing, so comparing two foundries by name says little, and each foundry picks its own baseline for the density gains it claims.

aka: GB200 NVL72, GB300 NVL72, Vera Rubin NVL72
plain: Nvidia's rack-sized product, with 72 accelerators in 18 compute trays joined through nine switch trays into one machine that software can treat as a single computer. The GB300 version draws up to 142 kilowatts.
why: AI capacity is now built and costed by the rack. SemiAnalysis puts the cost of owning a Vera Rubin NVL72 at $3.57 per GPU-hour, against $1.84 for a GB200 and $2.36 for a GB300.

aka: NVSwitch, NVLink 5, NVLink 6, NV-HBI
plain: Nvidia's own high-speed connection between its accelerators, carrying 3,600 gigabytes per second per GPU in NVLink 6, according to Nvidia's January 2026 Rubin launch, so that dozens of them can act as one.
why: Nvidia controls it, in a systems layer where most other parts have many suppliers. Since May 2025 its NVLink Fusion program has let other firms' custom chips, including CPUs from Fujitsu and Qualcomm, connect to Nvidia GPUs over NVLink, and UALink is a published open rival.

aka: optical module, pluggable optics, optical transceivers, transceiver, transceivers, optical modules, 800G optical transceivers
plain: A small device that turns electrical signals into laser light for sending down a glass fiber, and turns them back at the far end. Every network link longer than a few meters in a large AI cluster needs one at each end.
why: A cluster needs several for each accelerator, and one design for 100,000 H100s uses 98,304 just to link its GPUs to the first tier of switches. Chinese firms assemble the modules in volume, and only a few firms can make the lasers inside them, which is the narrow point.

aka: outsourced semiconductor assembly and test, OSATs, outsourced assembly and test, assembly and test firms, assembly and test contractor, assembly and test houses
plain: A contract firm that takes finished wafers, cuts them into chips, seals the chips into packages and tests them. It is the back end of chipmaking, done for hire.
why: Every chip passes through assembly and test, yet in the June 2026 quarter Amkor earned a gross margin of 16.8 percent and ASE's packaging and test segment 27.3 percent. Four of the ten largest firms by 2024 revenue are headquartered in China.

aka: overlay error, alignment
plain: How precisely one printed layer of a chip lands on top of the layer beneath it. Before each exposure the scanner finds marks printed in earlier layers and lines the new layer up on them to within a few nanometers, across a disc 300 millimeters wide.
why: Misalignment can ruin whole regions of a wafer, so overlay is one of the specifications that separates an advanced printing machine from an ordinary one. Each extra pass on a layer is another chance to misalign.

aka: pellicles, EUV pellicle
plain: A thin transparent membrane on a frame above a photomask so that dust settles on it, far enough out of focus that it does not print, and the pattern stays clean. It is a lens cap a photographer can shoot through.
why: Pellicles already work in high-volume EUV manufacturing, but no material is completely transparent to EUV light, and the light crosses the membrane twice, so every pellicle costs some output. Carbon nanotube membranes, which passed up to 97 percent of the light in one crossing in imec's 2020 tests, are the next step.

plain: An export control test of how densely a chip packs its computing power. It divides the chip's TPP, the export rules' measure of computing power, by its applicable die area in square millimeters, which counts all logic dies made on a process with non-planar transistors, and it applies only to a chip that reaches 1,600 TPP. It replaced the 2022 test, which was based on interconnect bandwidth, the speed at which a chip exchanges data with its neighbors.
why: It closed the gap used by Nvidia's China-specific chips, such as the A800 and H800, which had been designed around the 2022 interconnect-speed threshold. The top band, ECCN 3A090.a, now starts at 4,800 TPP, or at 1,600 TPP with a performance density of 5.92 (88 FR 73458).

aka: mask, reticle, mask set, photomasks, masks, mask sets, mask blank set
plain: The master template for one layer of a chip: a quartz plate, or for the shortest wavelengths a mirror, carrying the pattern that gets projected onto the wafer. A chip takes dozens of them, one per layer. In July 2022 SemiAnalysis put a full set above $1 million at 28 nm and above $10 million at 7 nm, and expected 3 nm sets to approach $40 million.
why: Mask cost decides which chips can afford a leading-edge process at all, and only three firms supply the blank plates for EUV masks, two of them Japanese.

aka: resist, resists, EUV resist, EUV resists, resist makers
plain: The light-sensitive coating that records a chip's pattern during lithography. A machine spins a thin film of it across the wafer, light through a stencil changes the film where it lands, and a wash removes those parts, much like developing photographic film. What remains shows the next machine where to etch.
why: Every printed layer of a chip passes through it, and each formula is approved for one layer of one product at one fab, so switching supplier takes years. Japanese companies held 78 percent of world sales in 2023, and a vehicle of a Japanese state-backed fund bought 84.36 percent of the resist maker JSR in 2024.

plain: A license review policy. An application may be filed and will be considered, but the reviewing agencies start from the position that it should be refused, and the exporter has to overcome that. It is the general policy for advanced computing chips going to China and Macau under 15 CFR 742.6(b)(10), and for most Entity List entries. Since January 2026 export applications for some lesser chips, such as the H200, are read case by case instead.
why: It is the distinction that decides whether a company files at all: under a presumption of denial an application can still be made, under a prohibition it cannot.

aka: probe cards
plain: A circuit board carrying thousands of fine needles that press down onto the contact pads of a chip while it is still part of the wafer, so a tester can drive signals into it. Every card is custom-built for one chip design.
why: Because cards are bespoke and slow to qualify, probe card supply and lead time set how fast a new accelerator or memory stack can ramp to volume.

aka: cabinet, racks, cabinets, rack-scale
plain: The standard steel frame that computing equipment is bolted into in a data center, roughly the size of a wardrobe. AI systems have turned the rack from a container into the product, because an entire rack is now sold and wired as one machine.
why: A GB300 NVL72 rack draws up to 142 kilowatts, and Nvidia's 800-volt design is drawn for racks of more than a megawatt from 2027. A megawatt rack changes the busbar, the floor loading, the coolant flow and the stored energy that carries the rack through a dip in power.

plain: Shipping an item that falls under US export rules, the EAR, from one foreign country to another, defined at 15 CFR 734.14. A memory stack subject to the EAR moving from Korea to China is a reexport, and it needs the same US license a shipment from Texas would.
why: The reexport rule lets US controls follow an item after it leaves the United States, which is what lets them reach trade between two foreign countries.

aka: photomask
plain: The patterned plate that a lithography machine projects onto the wafer, one chip layer at a time. In practice the word means the same as photomask, with reticle stressing that the machine steps the same image repeatedly across the disc.
why: The reticle's fixed printable area, 26 by 33 millimeters, is a hard physical limit that shapes how every large AI chip has to be designed.

aka: reticle size limit, reticle field, field size, reticle-limited, reticle size, reticles, times reticle
plain: The largest chip a lithography machine can print in a single exposure, about 858 square millimeters, or 26 by 33 millimeters. It is set by the machine's optics and is the same for every design.
why: Every AI accelerator worth buying needs more circuit than this, so designs are split into several dies and rejoined inside a package.

aka: back-end network, cluster fabric, scale-out, scale out
plain: The network that joins thousands of accelerator groups into one cluster, running at hundreds of gigabits per second over Ethernet or InfiniBand. The technology is ordinary data center networking; the scale is not.
why: It is how thousands of accelerators train one model together. InfiniBand was the main scale-out network when AI clusters were small, and Ethernet capacity has since grown quickly as Broadcom doubled the bandwidth of its switch chips every generation.

aka: scale-up fabric, coherent domain, scale-up, scale up, scale-up domain, scale-up switch
plain: The wiring that joins a few dozen accelerators inside one rack so a model too large for a single chip can be spread across them. It runs at terabytes per second, tens of times faster than the network between racks.
why: The group's bandwidth sets the size of model that can be trained. Nvidia sells its own NVLink for this layer, and UALink is a published open rival.

plain: The argument that Taiwan's dominance of advanced chipmaking deters an attack, because destroying or seizing TSMC would cost an aggressor and the world more than the island is worth.
why: The central and contested assumption behind Taiwan policy: a shield works only while it stays irreplaceable, which gives Taipei reason to slow the diversification its allies want.

aka: small yard with a high fence, small yard
plain: The stated design of US technology controls: restrict the narrow set of items that genuinely decide national security and leave the rest of the trade alone.
why: It gives critics and defenders a test for whether export controls remain targeted security policy or have become general industrial policy.

plain: The test for whether an item falls under US export rules at all. Under 15 CFR 734.3 it covers anything in the United States, anything of US origin wherever it now sits, foreign-made goods that contain more than a permitted share of controlled US content, and foreign-made goods caught by a foreign direct product rule. Nationality of the seller is not the test; the item is.
why: The phrase decides who the rules apply to. A Dutch or Korean firm shipping between two foreign countries can still need a US license, because the rules follow the item.

aka: substitutability rating
plain: A four-band rating of how hard it would be for a well-funded state or firm, starting today, to build an alternative to the leaders of a stage, judged against four written tests. Easy: a second supplier is qualified, meaning approved by customers, and shipping today at the leading node, the most advanced process. Moderate: a second supplier exists but is not yet qualified at the leading node, about two to five years to close the gap. Hard: no second supplier at the leading node, five to ten years, and the path is known. Very hard: no second supplier, and the path runs through physics, decades of unwritten know-how or protected intellectual property, ten years or more, and nobody has repeated it yet. The clock always times the same actor and stops at qualification, well after a prototype.
why: It says how long a rival or a government would need to replace a stage, which is the question the export debate turns on.

aka: package substrate, IC substrate, substrates, build-up substrate, build-up substrates, package substrates, IC substrates, resin substrate
plain: The small, dense circuit board that a chip package sits on, spreading the chip's microscopic connections out to the millimeter-scale solder balls a motherboard can accept. It is built up layer by layer from epoxy film, laser-drilled holes and plated copper.
why: A handful of Asian firms build these substrates for others, and as packages grow, warping and handling take over from the wiring in deciding what can be built.

aka: tape out, taped out, tapes out, tape-outs, tapeout
plain: The moment a chip design is declared finished and the pattern files are sent to the factory to be written into masks. The name survives from when the data physically left on a reel of magnetic tape.
why: After tape-out each revision needs at least some new masks, and in July 2022 SemiAnalysis expected a full 3 nm set to approach $40 million, so designers check everything they can before it.

aka: total processing performance
plain: The measure US export rules use for a chip's computing power: twice the number of multiply-accumulate operations, a multiply followed by an add, that it does each second, multiplied by the number of bits in each operation, added up across every processing unit on the chip. The definition sits in ECCN 3A090, in supplement no. 1 to 15 CFR part 774.
why: It is the dividing line for sales to China. The top band, 3A090.a, starts at 4,800 TPP, or at 1,600 with a performance density of 5.92, and since 15 January 2026 export applications for chips below 21,000 TPP and 6,500 GB/s of total DRAM bandwidth, such as the H200, are read case by case for end users in China and Macau (91 FR 1684).

aka: Tensor Processing Unit, TPUs
plain: Google's own AI chip, designed in-house for its data centers and cloud service. The seventh generation is called Ironwood.
why: It shows that a large buyer can design its own alternative to chips sold on the open market. Ironwood carries 192 GB of memory per chip, six times its predecessor's, with twice the performance per watt.

aka: transistors
plain: The switch every chip is built from. Current runs through a channel between two terminals, and a voltage on a third terminal, the gate, opens or closes that path much as a tap opens or closes a pipe. One Nvidia Blackwell part contains 208 billion of them.
why: Everything in this supply chain exists to make transistors smaller, faster and less leaky, and only three companies, TSMC, Intel and Samsung, make the newest kind in volume.

aka: through-silicon via, TSVs, through-silicon vias, through silicon via, through silicon vias
plain: A copper column drilled all the way down through a chip so that power and signals can pass from its top face to its bottom face. It is what makes stacking chips vertically possible, in the way an elevator shaft makes a tall building usable.
why: These columns are what make high bandwidth memory possible, and US rules control the tools that cut them by hole shape and etching speed.

aka: Validated End-User, Validated End User, Validated End-User status, VEU status, VEU cover, validated end users
plain: An authorization BIS grants to a named foreign facility, letting approved items ship to it without an individual license each time. The approved facilities are listed in supplement no. 7 to 15 CFR part 748, and the procedure is 15 CFR 748.15.
why: It let the China subsidiaries of Samsung and SK hynix, and the Dalian NAND fab that SK hynix bought from Intel, receive US equipment without individual licenses. BIS revoked that status effective 31 December 2025, and said it would license those fabs to keep running but not to expand capacity or upgrade technology (90 FR 42321). In December 2025 BIS granted SK hynix an annual license to ship approved US equipment to its China fabs during 2026.

aka: silicon wafer, 300 mm wafer, wafers, silicon wafers, 300 mm wafers
plain: The polished disc of ultrapure silicon that chips are built on, 300 millimeters across. Hundreds of chips are printed on one disc and cut apart at the end.
why: A large AI die loses more silicon to each flaw, so AI chips need wafers nearly flawless and flat to the edge. The top five wafer makers serve around 75 percent of a market worth $11.4 billion in 2025.

aka: WFE, front-end equipment, equipment billings, wafer processing equipment, semiconductor equipment, chipmaking tools, chipmaking equipment
plain: The collective name for the machines that process wafers inside a fab: printing systems, deposition and etch chambers, cleaning tools and measurement systems. It excludes the packaging and test machines used afterwards.
why: Spending on it shows how much new chipmaking capacity is being built. World sales of all chipmaking equipment reached $135.1 billion in 2025, and wafer processing tools rose 12 percent.

aka: die yield, yields, packaging yield, package yield, stack yield
plain: The percentage of chips on a wafer that work. Flaws land at random, so the larger the chip the more likely it is to catch one, and yield falls steeply as chips get bigger.
why: Yield sets the cost of a working AI chip. Epoch AI models the Blackwell compute die at 40 to 70 percent good, centered on 60, and spreading the loss from packages that fail test adds about $1,000 to each B200.

aka: chemical mechanical polishing, chemical mechanical planarization, polishing slurry, polishing slurries, slurry, slurries, CMP slurry, CMP pads, planarization
plain: After each new layer goes onto a wafer, its surface is rubbed flat again with a pad and a liquid full of fine grit, the slurry. The step is called chemical mechanical polishing, or CMP. Without it the next layer would be printed on a surface too bumpy to focus on.
why: Each slurry is approved for one layer of one product at one fab. As of 2021 DuPont and Cabot Microelectronics held about 56 percent of a $790 million slurry market. Cabot, renamed CMC Materials in October 2020, was bought by Entegris in July 2022, and DuPont's electronics business became Qnity Electronics in November 2025.

aka: ion implanter, ion implanters, implant, implant layers, implantation
plain: A way of changing how silicon conducts by firing atoms into it. An ion implanter shoots charged atoms of boron, phosphorus or arsenic into the wafer so they lodge just under the surface, and the patches they land in conduct the way the design needs. It is the first step in building each transistor.
why: No transistor can be built without it. Implanters are export-controlled, and in February 2026 Applied Materials agreed to pay a penalty of about $252 million over implanters shipped to an Entity-Listed Chinese customer.

aka: epitaxial, epitaxial wafer, epitaxial wafers, epitaxial layer, epi
plain: Epitaxy grows a fresh layer of crystal on top of a wafer, atom by atom, so the new layer continues the crystal beneath it with almost no flaws. An epitaxial wafer is a plain wafer with that extra layer, and the transistors are built in that layer.
why: The transistors are built in that layer, so its quality sets how little the chip can leak. SEMI credits the 2025 rise in wafer shipments to AI demand for advanced epitaxial wafers in logic and polished wafers for high-bandwidth memory.

aka: polycrystalline silicon, electronic-grade polysilicon, semiconductor-grade polysilicon, polysilicon feedstock
plain: Polysilicon is silicon refined to purity but not yet grown into one crystal: gray rods made of many small crystals. It is the raw material that is melted down to pull the single crystal a wafer is cut from. The same material, at lower purity, goes into solar panels.
why: China made about 93 percent of the world's polysilicon in 2023, yet none of the five major suppliers of the electronic-grade kind that Siltronic names for 2025 is Chinese.

aka: electronic grade, semiconductor-grade, semiconductor grade, solar-grade, solar grade
plain: Electronic-grade silicon is refined until its metal impurities are no more than a few parts per billion, pure enough for chips. Solar-grade silicon is a less pure grade made for solar cells.
why: Every chip starts from it, and the Commerce Department found in 2026 that semiconductor-grade polysilicon makes up only 2.4 percent of global production. Siltronic names five major suppliers for 2025, Wacker, Hemlock, OCI, Tokuyama and Mitsubishi, none of them Chinese.

aka: immersion DUV, ArF immersion, immersion scanner, immersion scanners, immersion tools, immersion DUV scanners, immersion deep-ultraviolet
plain: An immersion scanner prints with a thin layer of ultrapure water between its lens and the wafer. Light bends more sharply through water than through air, so the same lens prints finer lines. It is the best that deep ultraviolet light can do, one step below extreme ultraviolet.
why: Immersion is the tier that Dutch export licensing covers, and Reuters reported in July 2026, citing one unnamed source, that a Chinese state-owned firm had started producing its own immersion scanners.

aka: argon fluoride, argon fluoride laser, 193 nm, 193-nanometer
plain: ArF is argon fluoride, the gas mixture inside the laser that gives deep ultraviolet scanners their 193-nanometer light. An ArF scanner, dry or immersion, prints most of the fine layers on any chip made without extreme ultraviolet.
why: ArF immersion was 42 percent of ASML's system sales in 2025, and it is the tier a Chinese state-owned firm was reported in July 2026 to be producing at home.

aka: krypton fluoride, krypton fluoride laser, 248 nm, 248-nanometer
plain: KrF is krypton fluoride, the gas in an older lithography laser that shines at 248 nanometers. KrF scanners print the coarser layers of a chip, where lines are far apart, and thick films for packaging.
why: KrF tools print coarser layers such as implant layers, and ASML sold 78 of them in 2025 in a tier where Canon also competes.

aka: g-line, i-line steppers, i-line scanners
plain: i-line is the coarsest lithography light still in use, 365 nanometers from a mercury lamp, named for one line in the lamp's spectrum. It prints the widest features on a chip and much of a package.
why: i-line is where SMEE, the established Chinese scanner maker, is strongest, and even there it holds about 4 percent of the world market.

aka: scanners, stepper, steppers, lithography scanner, lithography scanners, lithography machine, lithography system, lithography systems
plain: A scanner is the lithography machine itself: it holds the photomask up to a light source and projects a shrunken image of one layer onto the wafer, sweeping mask and wafer past each other in a narrow slit of light. An older stepper exposes the whole field at once instead of scanning. A standard EUV scanner sells for around $200 million.
why: ASML makes every EUV scanner in the world, so a rule aimed at its scanners reaches all advanced chipmaking.

aka: plasmas, plasma etch, plasma-enhanced, plasma source
plain: A plasma is a gas that an electric field has split into charged ions and neutral fragments called radicals. In a chip tool the radicals do most of the chemistry and the ions give etch its direction. Most etch steps and many deposition steps happen in a plasma inside a vacuum chamber, while batch furnaces run oxidation, low-pressure deposition and some atomic layer deposition mostly without one. The extreme ultraviolet light source is a plasma of vaporized tin.
why: Deposition and etch chambers are separate products built from similar vacuum, gas and radio-frequency parts, and export controls describe each tool by the process it is designed to run.

aka: electron-beam, e-beam, electron beams, multi-beam, multibeam, e-beam inspection, electron-beam metrology
plain: An electron beam is a stream of electrons focused to a spot far smaller than any spot of light. Fabs use it to write the pattern onto a photomask, to inspect wafers for defects light cannot see, and to measure line widths. A multi-beam tool fires many beams at once, because a single beam is slow.
why: Intel calls Austria's IMS Nanofabrication the established leader in the multi-beam writers that advanced EUV masks require, and since December 2024 US rules control wafer inspection tools that use two or more beams to find defects 21 nm across or smaller.

aka: mask writers, multi-beam writer, multi-beam writers, electron-beam writer, e-beam writer, mask writing
plain: A mask writer is the machine that draws a chip's pattern into the resist on a photomask blank with electrons. A single-beam writer flashes one shape at a time, while NuFlare's multi-beam writer for the most advanced masks controls 260,000 beams at once.
why: No new chip can be printed until its masks are written. Intel says advanced EUV requires multi-beam mask writers and calls Austria's IMS Nanofabrication the established leader in them, and Japan's NuFlare also sells them.

aka: mask blanks, EUV blank, EUV blanks, photomask blank, photomask blanks, blank plate, DUV blanks
plain: A mask blank is a photomask before any pattern is on it: a six-inch square of very flat glass carrying the coating the pattern will be cut into. For extreme ultraviolet the coating is a mirror of about forty pairs of ultrathin layers, and a particle buried in it cannot be repaired.
why: Only three firms supply EUV blanks, AGC says, two of them Japanese, and AGC spent more than a decade meeting the blank's requirements before mass production began in 2017.

aka: physical vapor deposition, sputtering, sputtering target, sputtering targets, sputter
plain: Physical vapor deposition, or PVD, coats a wafer by knocking atoms off a solid slab of metal, the sputtering target, in a vacuum so they fly across and land on the wafer as a thin film. It lays down the metal barriers and seed layers under a chip's copper wiring.
why: Every copper wire needs that barrier, because copper seeps into the insulator around it. JX Advanced Metals puts its own share of the world market for semiconductor sputtering targets at about 65 percent as of fiscal 2026.

aka: chemical vapor deposition, PECVD, plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition, MOCVD, CVD precursor, precursor, precursors
plain: Chemical vapor deposition, or CVD, grows a film by flowing gases over a hot wafer so they react on its surface and leave a solid layer behind. The plasma-enhanced version, PECVD, runs cooler. The gases used are called precursors.
why: CVD made up $11.2 billion of a $26.2 billion deposition tool market in 2025, most of it the plasma-enhanced kind. Chinese toolmakers rose from 2 to 7 percent of deposition between 2019 and 2024.

aka: dielectrics, dielectric etch, dielectric properties, insulator, insulating layer
plain: A dielectric is an insulator: a material that does not conduct, such as the glassy oxides and nitrides between a chip's wires or the epoxy in a package substrate. Dielectric etch cuts holes and trenches through those insulating layers so the wires can be laid in.
why: How much signal a dielectric absorbs sets how fast a substrate or circuit board can run, which is why laminate suppliers matter to AI systems.

aka: critical dimensions, CD, CD-SEM, critical-dimension, line width, line-width, line widths
plain: The critical dimension is the width of the finest printed feature on a layer, the number a lithography and etch step is judged by. A CD-SEM is an electron microscope built to measure it across a wafer without cutting anything.
why: It is how a fab tells whether each lithography and etch step came out the right width. Hitachi holds 71.9 percent of the tools that measure it, the one kind Japan leads.

aka: backside power, backside vias, PowerVia, Super Power Rail, backside power network
plain: Backside power delivery grinds a finished wafer thin and builds the wires that carry power on its underside, so the wiring above the transistors carries only signals. Power arrives through holes drilled up from below, clear of the crowded top.
why: Intel ships it on 18A and TSMC on A16; it is one of the few remaining ways to make a chip faster without shrinking the transistor.

aka: copper vias, vertical vias, vertical copper vias
plain: Vias are the small vertical holes, filled with metal, that connect one layer of wiring to the layer above or below it. A chip's wiring is full of them; an interposer has them through its whole thickness; a package substrate has them drilled by laser through each sheet of film.
why: Every added layer is another set of vias that can fail, which is why yield falls as packages and substrates grow.

aka: coater-developer, coater and developer, coater/developer track, track tool, track tools
plain: A coater/developer, or track, is the machine that spins a thin coat of photoresist onto the wafer before it enters the scanner and washes away the exposed parts after it comes out, so every printed layer passes through it twice.
why: No pattern can be printed without it, and Tokyo Electron's own results put its share of the market at 91 percent in 2025.

aka: lots, wafer lot, wafer lots, per lot
plain: A lot is the batch of wafers a fab moves through its machines together, usually 25 in one sealed carrier. Recipes, inspections and yield are tracked lot by lot.
why: How many wafers per lot a fab can afford to inspect is a cost decision that sets what process control costs it.

aka: front end of line, FEOL, front-end, front-end wafers
plain: The front end of line is the first half of making a chip, the steps that build the transistors in the silicon. In the industry at large, the front end means the whole wafer fab, as against the back end where chips are packaged and tested.
why: SemiAnalysis judged in March 2026 that front-end capacity had overtaken packaging as the main bottleneck on AI chip output, though TSMC said in July 2026 that its packaging capacity still limited customers' growth.

aka: back end of line, BEOL, back-end, back-end fabs, back-end tools
plain: Inside a fab, the back end of line is the second half of making a chip, the dozen or more layers of copper wiring stacked above the transistors. In the industry at large, the back end means everything after the wafer leaves the fab: grinding, dicing, packaging and test.
why: Wiring is now as hard to make as the transistor, and in the back end outside the fab, four of the ten largest assembly and test firms by 2024 revenue are headquartered in China.

aka: static random-access memory, cache, on-chip memory, on-die SRAM, on-die memory, L2 cache
plain: SRAM is the fast memory built from transistors on the logic chip itself, used as a cache that holds the numbers a processor is about to need. It is far faster than the memory stacks beside the chip and holds far less.
why: The cell that holds one bit has barely shrunk since the 5 nm node, which caps how much cache an accelerator can afford.

aka: HVM, volume production, mass production, high volume, in volume, production ramp
plain: High-volume manufacturing is the point where a new process or product stops being a trial and runs at full rate with enough good chips to sell.
why: Foundries announce the date a process reaches it, and before then the process runs only in trials such as risk production.

aka: ramps, ramp-up, ramping, yield at ramp
plain: A ramp is the months in which a new process or product climbs from a few wafers a week to full output while the share of working chips rises. Yield is lowest at the start of the ramp and improves as engineers find which steps lose dies.
why: Yield in the first year of a new process separates a profitable node from a subsidized one.

aka: thermocompression, thermo-compression bonding, thermocompression bonder, thermocompression bonders, TCB, die bonder, die bonders, bonder, bonders
plain: Thermocompression bonding presses one die onto another, or onto a substrate, under heat and force until the tiny solder bumps between them melt and join. It is how memory dies are stacked into an HBM cube and how chiplets are placed on a package.
why: ASMPT says it remained the leader in these bonders in 2025, when its thermocompression bonder revenue rose about 146 percent, and it aims for 35 to 40 percent of a market it puts at $1.6 billion in 2028.

aka: wafer dicing, dicing saw, dicing saws, grinding, wafer grinding, grinders, wafer grinders, thinning, wafer thinning
plain: Dicing cuts a finished wafer into its individual dies with a diamond saw or a laser. Grinding, done first, thins the wafer from the back, and for stacked memory it goes on until the copper columns inside the dies come through.
why: HBM depends on that grinding, and Disco of Japan leads in wafer grinders and dicing saws.

aka: panel-level, panel level packaging, rectangular panel, rectangular panels
plain: Panel-level packaging builds packages on a large rectangular sheet instead of a round wafer, so far less area is wasted at the edges and many more packages fit on one carrier. It is the industry's way around the size limits of a 300 mm wafer.
why: Powertech aims to run the first panel-level packaging line for AI chips in 2027.

aka: wafer test, probe test, wafer probe
plain: Wafer sort is the first test a chip gets, while it is still on the wafer. A probe card lowers thousands of needles onto the pads of one die, a tester drives signals in and reads the answers, and any die that answers wrong is marked and never packaged.
why: Proving a die good before it is packaged keeps one bad die from scrapping the memory stacks and substrate it would be joined to.

aka: burn in, wafer-level burn-in, burn-in test
plain: Burn-in runs a chip hot and at raised voltage for minutes to days so that anything that would have failed early fails in the factory, before the part is shipped. It can run on the wafer or in the package, and Aehr's lead AI customer is moving it for its accelerators from the finished system to the wafer.
why: One weak die in a package of a dozen expensive parts scraps all of them, so burn-in now protects everything else in the package.

aka: qualify, qualifies, qualified, qualifying, requalify, requalification, qualification tests, qualification lock-in
plain: Qualification is the testing a fab or a customer runs before it will accept a new material, tool or supplier for one product. A resist, a slurry, a wafer source or a memory stack is approved for one layer of one product at one fab, and switching means running the whole test again.
why: Qualification is what makes a second source take years, and it protects incumbent suppliers.

aka: second sources, second-source, multi-sourcing, dual source, single source, sole source, single-source
plain: A second source is a second supplier qualified for the same part or material, so that a fab can keep running if the first one stops shipping. A single-source part has none, and adding one means joint development and a fresh qualification.
why: A second source lets a fab keep running when one supplier is cut off. When Japan put three chemicals under export licenses for South Korea in 2019, Korea bought more from other countries and output of all three rose at Korean firms and at Japanese companies' affiliates in Korea.

aka: mask shops, mask making, mask maker, mask makers
plain: A mask shop is the factory, inside a foundry or run by a specialist such as Photronics, that turns a finished chip design into its set of photomasks. It writes each plate with an electron beam, inspects it and repairs it.
why: No chip can be printed until its masks are made. Chipmakers such as TSMC and SMIC run shops of their own, and independents such as Photronics sell to them and to others.

aka: silicon IP, IP blocks, licensed blocks, licensed circuit blocks, semiconductor IP, IP catalog, intellectual property
plain: In chip design, IP means a ready-made block of circuitry, such as a processor core or a memory interface, that a design house licenses. Arm sells processor IP; others sell the blocks that talk to memory, PCIe or another chiplet.
why: Each licensed block must be proven on a new process before a chip can use it, and the memory interface is a demanding block, because it has to hold its timing across thousands of solder bumps into a stacked memory die.

aka: register-transfer level, register-transfer-level, register transfer level, RTL description, RTL code
plain: RTL, for register-transfer level, is the code in which a chip is first written: a text description, in a language such as SystemVerilog, of what every storage element holds on every tick of the clock. Software later turns it into transistors and wires.
why: It fixes what the chip does, so a large team checks it in simulation and emulation before tape-out, because a mistake found later needs new masks.

aka: sign-off, static timing analysis, timing signoff, timing sign-off, physical verification, signed off
plain: Signoff is the final set of automated checks a chip design must pass before a foundry will make it: that every signal arrives in time at the clock speed promised, and that every shape in the layout can be printed. Static timing analysis is the timing half; physical verification is the layout half.
why: Synopsys holds more than 90 percent of timing signoff and Siemens more than 85 percent of physical verification, and a foundry accepts only designs that have passed these checks.

aka: process design kit, process design kits
plain: A process design kit, or PDK, is the file set a foundry gives designers describing exactly what its factory can print: the sizes, spacings and electrical behavior of every feature on one node. Design software is checked against it before a chip is accepted.
why: A foundry validates each exact version of the design software against its kit, and it refuses signoff from a version it has not validated.

aka: RISC-V cores, RISC-V processor
plain: RISC-V is an open instruction set, the list of basic commands a processor understands, that anyone may use without a license. Companies build their own processor cores on it, and Nvidia now uses such cores for housekeeping inside every GPU.
why: It is the license-free alternative to Arm's processor designs, and it handles the small control tasks on chips such as every Nvidia GPU.

aka: PCI Express, PCIe 6, PCIe 7
plain: PCIe is the standard connector and link that joins a processor to the cards inside a computer, an accelerator included. In an AI server it carries data between the host processor and the GPUs, while faster private links join the GPUs to each other.
why: The PCIe block is licensed IP that has to be proven on each new node before a chip can use it.

aka: Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express, UCIe 3.0
plain: UCIe is an open standard for the short, very fast link between two chiplets sitting side by side in one package. It lets chiplets from different vendors be wired together, the way PCIe lets cards from different vendors share a computer.
why: Accelerators too large to print as one chip are built from chiplets, and a shared standard lets more firms supply the pieces.

aka: serializer-deserializer, high-speed serial links, serial links, serial link
plain: A SerDes, for serializer-deserializer, is the circuit at the edge of a chip that turns many slow parallel signals into one very fast stream over a single wire, and back again at the other end. Every link out of an accelerator, to another chip, a switch or an optical module, runs through one.
why: SerDes speed sets how much data a chip can move, and the blocks are licensed IP that has to be proven in silicon on each new process.

aka: microbumps, solder bump, solder bumps, bumps, bump, bump metrology
plain: A microbump is a dot of solder that joins a die to the interposer or substrate beneath it. Microbumps sit 30 to 40 microns apart, about a third of a hair's width, and each one is an electrical connection that has to survive the package heating and cooling.
why: Their spacing limits how many connections fit between stacked or neighboring chips. Hybrid bonding, copper pressed straight onto copper, would pack them far closer, and it is not yet ready for HBM.

aka: RDL, redistribution wiring, redistribution layers
plain: A redistribution layer is a thin sheet of fine copper wiring, laid down in resin, that spreads a die's tightly spaced connections out to a wider pattern the package can handle. CoWoS-R and CoWoS-L use it in place of a full silicon interposer.
why: Swapping silicon for redistribution wiring is how TSMC pushed packages past 3.3 times the reticle size.

aka: silicon bridges, EMIB, silicon-bridge, local silicon bridges, embedded bridge
plain: A silicon bridge is a small sliver of silicon carrying dense wiring, set into the package only where two dies need thousands of connections between them, so the rest of the package can use cheaper wiring. Intel calls its version EMIB; TSMC's CoWoS-L uses the same idea.
why: Bridges let a package grow past a single interposer's size limit, which is how CoWoS-L carries Blackwell and Rubin. The bridges in Blackwell needed very high placement accuracy, and packaging issues limited its supply.

aka: PCB, PCBs, printed circuit boards, circuit board, circuit boards, high-multilayer PCB
plain: A printed circuit board is the flat green or black card that electronic parts are soldered onto, with its wiring etched from copper sheets and stacked in layers. Boards for AI servers can run past 30 layers.
why: It carries the power and the links between GPUs, and how much signal its laminate absorbs is now a main design limit.

aka: laminates, copper-clad laminate, copper-clad laminates, low-loss laminate, core laminate
plain: A laminate is a stiff sheet made by pressing glass cloth and resin together, usually with copper foil bonded to its faces. It is the material a circuit board or a substrate core is cut from. A low-loss laminate absorbs little of the signal passing through the wires on it.
why: How much signal the laminate absorbs has become a main design limit on the boards that link GPUs.

aka: T-glass, low-expansion glass, glass fiber cloth, low-expansion glass cloth
plain: Glass cloth is a woven fabric of fine glass fibers that gives a substrate core or circuit board its stiffness. T-glass is a special grade that barely expands when heated, which keeps a large package flat.
why: Nitto Boseki of Japan claims an overwhelming advantage in low-expansion glass cloth, and says demand seems to have risen about two to three times since its fiscal 2024 to 2027 plan was set.

aka: CTE, thermal expansion, expansion mismatch, low-CTE
plain: The coefficient of thermal expansion is how much a material swells for each degree it warms. Silicon barely moves, epoxy moves more, and when the two are bonded and heated, the package bends.
why: Matching expansion across die, bridge, interposer and substrate is what warpage control means, and it gets harder as packages grow.

aka: base chip, base logic die, logic base die, HBM base die
plain: The base die is the bottom chip of an HBM stack, the one that manages the memory dies above it and talks to the processor on their behalf. For HBM4, SK hynix moved it to TSMC's advanced logic process so it can hold more functions. Samsung's HBM4, shipped from February 2026, uses a 4 nm logic base die.
why: SK hynix made its own base dies up to HBM3E, so the move gives TSMC a role inside a product it does not make.

aka: 3D NAND, NAND flash, flash memory, 128-layer NAND
plain: NAND is the memory that keeps data when the power is off: the storage inside a phone, a laptop drive or a data center disk. 3D NAND stacks its cells in many layers, made by etching holes far deeper than they are wide. It is slow next to DRAM and is not used inside an AI accelerator.
why: The October 2022 US rules set one fab threshold at 128-layer NAND, and the proposed MATCH Act would name YMTC, a Chinese maker of it, in statute.

aka: JESD270-4, JEDEC standard
plain: JEDEC is the industry body that writes the standards for memory chips, so that a memory stack from any maker fits any processor built to the same specification. Its HBM4 standard, published in April 2025, sets the width and speed of the interface.
why: Makers now ship HBM4 faster than the standard's 8 Gb/s per pin, Samsung at 11.7, SK hynix above 10 and Micron above 11, and each customer runs its own qualification tests, so meeting the standard does not by itself win an order.

aka: bandwidth density, bandwidth-density
plain: Memory bandwidth density is how much data a memory stack can move each second divided by the area of its package or stack, in gigabytes per second per square millimeter. The December 2024 rule controls any stack above 2, and BIS said every HBM stack then in production exceeded that.
why: One threshold catches every HBM stack in production, including stacks made outside the United States, so the control reaches all three makers. A license exception still lets stacks below 3.3 go straight to a chip designer's packaging site, and HBM already packaged with a processor falls under the chip rules instead.

aka: baseboards, SXM, OAM, accelerator module, HGX, HGX baseboard
