plain: A baseboard is the large circuit board that eight accelerator modules bolt onto inside a server, carrying their power and the switch chips that let them reach each other at full speed. Nvidia's module is called SXM and its baseboard HGX; the open-standard equivalents are OAM and UBB.
why: The eight-module baseboard makes the server the unit of compute, and rack-scale systems such as the NVL72 drop it to join 72 GPUs through switch trays in the rack.

aka: Quantum-2, Quantum-X800
plain: InfiniBand is a networking standard built for supercomputers, with low delay and no dropped packets, that AI clusters used to link thousands of servers before Ethernet caught up. Nvidia sells both.
why: The choice between InfiniBand and Ethernet decides who sells the switch chips, and Broadcom's Ethernet parts now double in bandwidth every generation.

aka: Ultra Ethernet, Spectrum-X, Spectrum-X Ethernet, Tomahawk, Ethernet switch
plain: Ethernet is the ordinary networking standard of offices and the internet, now made fast and reliable enough to link the servers of an AI cluster. The switch chips at its heart, such as Broadcom's Tomahawk, route traffic between thousands of accelerators.
why: Broadcom has doubled the bandwidth of the Ethernet switch chips it sells to all comers every generation, from 25.6 Tbps on one chip in Tomahawk 4 to 102.4 in Tomahawk 6.

aka: co-packaged, co-packaging, CPO, plug-in modules, plug-in optics
plain: Co-packaged optics puts the lasers and light-to-electricity converters onto the switch chip's own package instead of into plug-in modules at the front of the box.
why: The optics' power cost is one reason Broadcom and Nvidia are moving them onto the switch package, and Broadcom says its Tomahawk 6 Davisson cuts optical interconnect power by 70 percent.

aka: InP, indium
plain: Indium phosphide is a crystal, grown from the metal indium and phosphorus, that gives off light when current passes through it, which silicon cannot do. It is the material of the lasers inside the fastest optical modules.
why: China produces about 70 percent of the world's indium and put it under new export restrictions in February 2025, when it also began requiring export permits for indium phosphide substrates. In March 2026 Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion each in Coherent and Lumentum, alongside purchase commitments for their lasers.

aka: busbars, copper busbar, copper busbars
plain: A busbar is a thick bar of solid copper that carries very large currents down the back of a rack to the boards that need them, doing the job a cable would melt trying to do. The busbars feeding a single AI rack can weigh 200 kilograms.
why: Nvidia is moving to 800-volt distribution so the same copper carries over 150 percent more power and those heavy bars are no longer needed.

aka: power shelves, rack power shelf
plain: A power shelf is a slide-in unit in a rack that converts the incoming supply to the voltage the boards use and feeds it to the busbar. A GB300 NVL72 rack draws its 142 kilowatts through eight of them at 33 kilowatts each.
why: The shelves and the boards behind them have many suppliers; the transformers upstream do not.

aka: large power transformers, transformer, transformers, switchgear, substation
plain: A large power transformer is the machine that steps grid electricity down from transmission voltage to a level a data center can use. Switchgear is the heavy switching and protection equipment around it, and together they make up the substation at the gate of the campus.
why: Lead times of 36 months are commonly quoted, against under a year before the pandemic, and 82 percent of the units put into US service in 2019 were imported.

aka: square millimeters, square millimeter, mm²
plain: mm2 means square millimeters, the unit chip areas are given in. A lithography scanner prints at most 858 mm2 in one shot, each compute die in an Nvidia B200 is about 800 mm2, and TSMC's interposer planned for 2028 is roughly 12,000 mm2, about the area of a compact disc.
why: Yield falls faster than area rises, so die area drives the cost of each working chip.

aka: kW, kilowatts, megawatt, MW, megawatts, gigawatt, GW, gigawatts
plain: A kilowatt is a thousand watts. A megawatt is a thousand kilowatts, and a gigawatt a thousand megawatts, about the output of one large power station. A GB300 NVL72 rack draws up to 142 kilowatts; a data center campus is now sized in gigawatts.
why: AI deals and campuses are now counted in gigawatts, as when OpenAI and Broadcom announced 10 gigawatts of accelerators, and power equipment now arrives more slowly than the chips.

aka: terawatt-hour, terawatt-hours, terawatt hours
plain: A terawatt-hour is a billion kilowatt-hours, the unit national electricity use is counted in. US data centers used 176 TWh in 2023, 4.4 percent of the country's electricity.
why: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects 325 to 580 TWh by 2028, between 6.7 and 12 percent of US electricity.

aka: TB/s, Gb/s, Tbps, gigabytes per second, terabytes per second, gigabits per second, terabits per second
plain: GB/s is gigabytes per second, the measure of how much data a link or a memory can move; TB/s is a thousand times more. A lowercase b, as in Gb/s or Tbps, counts bits, each an eighth of a byte. One HBM4 stack moves over 2 TB/s; NVLink 6 gives each GPU 3,600 GB/s, according to Nvidia's January 2026 Rubin launch.
why: The October 2022 US rule caught chips with a processing score of 4,800 or more and an input and output rate of 600 GB/s or more (87 FR 62186), and since January 2026 chips below 6,500 GB/s of total DRAM bandwidth and 21,000 TPP can be licensed case by case for China (91 FR 1684).

aka: wafers a month, wafer starts, wafer starts per month, WSPM, wafer starts a month, million wafers per month
plain: Wafers per month is how fab capacity is counted: the number of wafers a plant can start through its line each month. A TSMC gigafab runs more than 100,000, and SMIC's capacity at 7 nm and below was conservatively estimated at 45,000 a month at the end of 2025. Figures are often converted to 8-inch or 12-inch equivalents so plants with different wafer sizes can be compared.
why: SEMI forecast China at 10.1 million wafers a month in 2025, the most of any region, but little of that capacity is advanced.

aka: 300-millimeter, 12-inch, 12-inch equivalent, 200 mm, 8-inch, 8-inch-equivalent, 450 mm, 150 mm
plain: 300 mm is the diameter of the standard wafer, about twelve inches. Older fabs run 200 mm, or 8-inch, wafers. The last increase in wafer size, to 300 mm, came in 2002.
why: 300 mm wafers carried 99.7 percent of world fab capacity at 45 nm and below in SEMI's November 2020 World Fab Forecast, which CSET cited in January 2021, so advanced chips start on them.

aka: nm, nanometers, microns, micrometer, micrometers, angstrom, angstroms, picometer, picometers
plain: A nanometer is a billionth of a meter. A micron, or micrometer, is a thousand nanometers, an angstrom is a tenth of a nanometer, and a picometer is a thousandth. Lithography light is measured in nanometers, package bumps in microns, and mirror flatness in picometers.
why: Node names such as 2 nm no longer describe any feature that size, but the physical limits of printing and stacking are still set in these units.

aka: pitches, half-pitch, gate pitch, metal pitch, wire pitch, line pitch
plain: Pitch is the distance from one line on a chip to the next, center to center, so it counts the line and the gap together. Half-pitch is half that. A 16 nm pitch means lines 16 nanometers apart; the 2022 rules set a DRAM threshold at 18 nm half-pitch.
why: Pitch measures something physical on the chip, which a node name does not, though SemiAnalysis calls a single pitch an incomplete metric for comparing processes.

aka: 5 nm-class, 7 nm-class, 2 nm-class, nanometer-class, nm class
plain: Nm-class, as in 7 nm-class, means a process roughly as dense as the foundries' 7 nm generation, used when a maker's own name for the node is different or when nothing on it measures 7 nanometers.
why: SMIC builds its 7 nm-class processes without extreme ultraviolet machines, and its most advanced, N+3, reaches the density of TSMC's 6 nm-class process.

aka: logic density, chip density, transistors per square millimeter, density gain
plain: Transistor density is how many transistors fit in a square millimeter of chip. SemiAnalysis measured SMIC's N+3 at 113.4 million, against 107.7 million for TSMC's N6. TSMC says N2P gives 1.2 times the logic density and 1.15 times the chip density of N3E. A16, which adds backside power, gives up to 1.10 times the chip density of N2P, and A14 more than 20 percent more logic density than N2.
why: Density sets how much logic fits on a die of a given size. No foundry publishes wafer prices, so cost per transistor cannot be worked out from public figures.

aka: wafers an hour, wafers per hour, wafers-per-hour
plain: Throughput is how many wafers a machine can process in an hour. ASML's NXE:3800E EUV scanner reaches 220.
why: Throughput sets the cost of each layer and how many lots a fab can afford to inspect, which is why brighter EUV light sources and multi-beam inspection tools matter.

aka: utilization rate, fab utilization
plain: Utilization is how full a fab's lines are running, as a share of what they could run. A fab costs the same whether it is full or empty, so utilization decides whether it makes money.
why: SMIC ran its lines 93.5 percent full in 2025, and its gross margin that year was 21 percent.

aka: operating profit, operating loss, operating income
plain: Operating margin is what is left of revenue after both the cost of making the product and the cost of running the company, research and sales included, as a share of revenue. It sits below gross margin, which counts only the cost of making.
why: SK hynix's earnings release gives no gross margin, so its operating margin, 76 percent in the June 2026 quarter, is the public measure of how much it keeps from memory sales.

aka: lead times, delivery time
plain: Lead time is the wait between placing an order and receiving it. A wafer clears a leading-edge fab in months, while a large power transformer commonly takes three years.
why: Chip supply and power equipment are both constrained. Micron said in its report for the quarter to May 2026 that AI-driven memory and storage growth was outpacing industry supply, and waits for large power equipment run to years.

aka: oligopolies, duopoly, three-firm oligopoly
plain: An oligopoly is a market with only a few sellers, so each one's decisions move the price; a duopoly has two. DRAM, industrial gases, substrates and chip testers are all oligopolies.
why: The fewer the sellers, the more one accident or one license decision moves the market, and with a single seller, losing it stops the line.

aka: leading-edge, at the leading edge, advanced node, advanced nodes, advanced-node
plain: The leading edge is the newest generation of chipmaking process in volume production, today the 3 nm and 2 nm nodes, made only by TSMC, Samsung and Intel. A leading-edge chip is one built on it. Everything older is a mature node.
why: Only TSMC, Intel and Samsung make gate-all-around transistors in volume, and in 2024 the United States put a worldwide license requirement on the technology for building them.

aka: mature nodes, mature-node, mature logic, older nodes, older lines, trailing edge
plain: A mature node is an older chipmaking process, 28 nm and above, that has run for years and competes on price. Most of the world's wafers come off these lines, making power chips, analog parts and microcontrollers.
why: China held 33 percent of the world's logic capacity at 28 nm and above in 2022, and its mature-node chipmaking is going domestic on a visible timetable.

aka: original design manufacturer, ODMs, contract manufacturer, contract manufacturers, contract manufacturing, EMS, server ODM
plain: An ODM, for original design manufacturer, is a firm such as Foxconn, Quanta or Wistron that designs and builds servers and racks to a customer's specification and puts the customer's name on the box. A contract manufacturer does the assembly only.
why: Several contract manufacturers on three continents can build an AI rack, and moving Foxconn's share to Quanta and Wistron would take an estimated several quarters. Nvidia said in its filing for the quarter to April 2026 that the complexity of rack-scale systems had caused production delays.

aka: inference chip, inference chips, inference accelerator, inference accelerators, training and inference
plain: Running a finished AI model to answer requests, such as a prompt. Training, a run of weeks on a cluster of accelerators, builds the model first. To write each word of an answer, the chip reads the whole model from memory, does a little arithmetic and waits for the next read. Training reuses each number it fetches, so it fetches little and computes a lot.
why: Inference is where memory size and speed usually set how many people one chip can serve.

aka: weights, frontier model weights, trained weights
plain: Model weights are the billions of numbers an AI model consists of once it has been trained, the file that runs on the chips. Copy the weights and the model goes with them.
why: A chip reads every weight from memory for each word it writes, so bigger models need more HBM. The AI Diffusion rule made frontier weights a controlled item, ECCN 4E091, reaching past the chips to what they produce.

aka: export controls, export licensing, export license, export licenses, export licence, export licences, export-control
plain: An export control is a rule that makes a sale need the government's permission. The government names an item and a buyer, and from then on its own companies must hold a license before they ship that item to that buyer. The United States stretches the rule to goods made abroad with American technology.
why: It works only when the seller's firms make something the buyer cannot get elsewhere, and each chapter tests that condition for one stage of the chain.

plain: 3A090 is the entry in the US export control list that covers advanced AI chips, defined by their total processing performance and performance density; 4A090 covers the computers built from them. Its part c, added in December 2024, covers high bandwidth memory. A chip inside 3A090.a needs a license for China, and the AI Diffusion rule of January 2025 extended that requirement to every destination, though BIS says it enforces it only for Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 and for firms headquartered in D:5 or Macau.
why: It decides which AI chips need a license for China, so designers now build chips around its thresholds.

plain: 3B001 and 3B090 are the entries in the US export control list that cover chipmaking equipment, written as process specifications: an etch tool that cuts sideways, a deposition tool that reaches 200-to-1 holes. The related 3D and 3E entries cover the software and know-how that go with the tools.
why: They decide which chipmaking tools need an export license, and they describe what a tool can do, since the same chamber can add or remove material depending on its recipe.

aka: affiliates rule, 50 percent rule, affiliates of listed entities
plain: The Affiliates Rule extended the Entity List to any company at least half owned by a listed firm, anywhere in the world, so that a listed company could not buy through a subsidiary. It took effect on 29 September 2025 and was suspended for a year six weeks later.
why: It is stayed to 9 November 2026, and if it returns, subsidiaries at least half owned by listed firms will again need licenses.

aka: US persons, U.S. person, U.S. persons
plain: In export law a US person is any American citizen, resident or company, wherever in the world they are. Since October 2022 a US person may not service or support an advanced chip fab in China without a license.
why: The rule reaches people as well as goods, so American citizens, residents and companies need a license to support advanced chipmaking in China.

aka: consignees, named consignee, named consignees, ultimate consignee
plain: The consignee is the party a shipment is sent to, the name on the export license. A named consignee, such as G42 in the United Arab Emirates, can receive controlled chips on the terms attached to its own name.
why: The July 2026 UAE rule names the Emirati government, G42 and US-headquartered AI companies as consignees who can take controlled AI chips without a license, so the favorable treatment is tied to the named buyers.

aka: approval is presumed, presumed approval
plain: A presumption of approval means a license is still required but will normally be granted. It is the opposite of a presumption of denial, and the two can sit inside one rule. HBM license applications for Macau and Country Group D:5 are presumed approved when neither the buyer nor its ultimate parent is headquartered in either place, and presumed denied otherwise (15 CFR 742.6(b)(10)(ii)).
why: The split lets HBM reach plants in China owned by firms headquartered elsewhere while holding it back from Chinese-owned buyers.

aka: case by case, case-by-case, reviewed case by case
plain: Case-by-case review means a license is required and each application is judged on its own, with no presumption either way. Since January 2026 the H200 and MI325X are reviewed this way for China, with conditions attached to each approval.
why: It is the middle setting between an open market and a presumption of denial, and it is where the current settlement sits.

aka: AIA, Artificial Intelligence Authorization
plain: License Exception AIA, for Artificial Intelligence Authorization, lets the top band of AI chips ship without a license to the nineteen destinations, the United States among them, listed in supplement no. 5 to part 740. The AI Diffusion rule created it in January 2025 as the exception inside a worldwide license requirement.
why: BIS said in May 2025 that it would not enforce the rule, but the rule was never repealed, so AIA still stands in the regulations. BIS says it enforces the worldwide requirement only for Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 and for firms headquartered in D:5 or Macau.

aka: ACM, Advanced Compute Manufacturing
plain: License Exception ACM, for Advanced Compute Manufacturing, lets controlled AI chips and related items go without a license to private-sector firms that develop, make or store them, as long as the items are bound for customers outside Macau and Country Group D:5. It is a sibling of AIA and LPP.
why: It keeps the AI Diffusion rule's worldwide license requirement from catching chips that are only passing through factories and warehouses on their way to an eligible customer.

aka: AI Diffusion, diffusion rule, Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, AI Diffusion framework
plain: The AI Diffusion rule, published on 15 January 2025, required a license to ship the most capable AI chips anywhere in the world, then opened exceptions: unlimited to nineteen destinations, capped volumes elsewhere, nothing to China. It also controlled the weights of frontier AI models.
why: Four months later BIS said it would leave the rule unenforced, and it withdrew none of the text, so its license requirement and exceptions still stand in the regulations. BIS says it enforces the requirement only for Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 and for firms headquartered in D:5 or Macau.

aka: FR, 89 FR, 91 FR, 88 FR, Federal Register notice
plain: The Federal Register is the US government's daily journal, where every new rule is published before it takes effect. A citation such as 89 FR 96790 means volume 89, page 96790. Export control rules appear there first, and the page number is how they are cited.
why: US export rules change by notices published there, with no act of Congress needed.

aka: CFR, Code of Federal Regulations, 15 CFR 742.6, part 742, part 740, part 734, supplement no. 5 to part 740, supplement no. 5
plain: The Code of Federal Regulations is the standing text of US rules, sorted into titles and parts. Title 15 holds the Export Administration Regulations: part 734 says what is subject to them, part 740 lists the license exceptions and, in its supplement no. 5, the nineteen destinations eligible for License Exception AIA, and part 742 sets the licensing policy for each control.
why: A rule announced in the Federal Register stays in the CFR until it is removed, which is why the unenforced AI Diffusion rule still stands in the regulations.

aka: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry
plain: METI is Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, the ministry that writes Japan's export controls and funds its chip industry. It put advanced chipmaking equipment under export license from July 2023 and supports Rapidus and mask-blank capacity.
why: Japan's controls apply to every destination and name no country, and METI is the office that decides them.

aka: Ministry of Commerce, China's Ministry of Commerce
plain: MOFCOM is China's Ministry of Commerce, the ministry that writes and administers China's own export controls. Its notices put gallium, germanium and seven rare earths under license, and in December 2024 it banned exports of gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials to the United States.
why: Beijing's retaliation targets inputs such as these minerals, and MOFCOM signs each notice.

aka: CHIPS and Science Act, CHIPS incentives, CHIPS money, CHIPS Act grants, CHIPS authorization, CHIPS Act support, CHIPS award
plain: The CHIPS and Science Act authorized about $52.7 billion of US federal money for the chip industry. By July 2025 Commerce had awarded $30.9 billion of direct funding to 19 companies for 40 projects.
why: Its grants paid a median 14.2 percent of each funded project's capital cost, and in August 2025 $5.7 billion of unpaid Intel grants went into the government's $8.9 billion purchase of a 9.9 percent stake in Intel.

aka: National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, National Integrated Circuit Fund, third chip fund, China's third chip fund
plain: The Big Fund is the nickname for China's National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, the state vehicle that puts government money into Chinese chip firms. Its third round, raised in May 2024, came to 344 billion yuan, about $47 billion.
why: CSIS puts China's cumulative state funding for chips since 2014 at an estimated $150 billion, and the money has produced a domestic tool industry and no leading-edge node.

aka: Macao, China or Macau, China and Macau
plain: Macau is a Chinese city with its own customs territory, like Hong Kong, so goods can enter it under separate rules. US export controls name China and Macau together to close that route, and treat a firm headquartered in either the same way.
why: US chip rules name China and Macau together, which is why the pair appears throughout the AI Chips page.

aka: specialty gas, electronic specialty gases, bulk gases, bulk gas, electronic gases, process gas, process gases
plain: The gases a fab uses in small amounts, each for one job, such as silane, which carries silicon into the chamber to build a film, or nitrogen trifluoride, which cleans the chamber. They arrive in cylinders by the gram. Bulk gases, such as nitrogen and oxygen, arrive by the metric ton and are often made on the fab site.
why: Specialty gases travel in cylinders, so a government or a war can cut them off. Ukraine supplied about 70 percent of the world's neon before Russia invaded in 2022.

aka: hydrofluoric acid, HF, ultra-high-purity hydrofluoric acid, high-purity hydrogen fluoride
plain: Hydrogen fluoride is a gas that dissolves glass, and hydrofluoric acid is its solution in water. Fabs use both to strip oxide layers and clean wafers between steps, at purities of about one stray metal atom in a trillion.
why: When Japan put it under individual export licenses for South Korea in 2019, its exports to Korea fell 87.9 percent, and Korea bought more from the United States and Taiwan and made more at home.

aka: NF3
plain: Nitrogen trifluoride is a gas that, split apart in a plasma, releases fluorine that scours the deposits off the inside of a process chamber between wafers.
why: A shortage of any one chemical can stop a fab, and nitrogen trifluoride is the specialty of smaller firms such as SK Materials of Korea.

aka: neon gas, semiconductor-grade neon
plain: Neon is the gas inside the lasers that give deep ultraviolet scanners their light, mixed with krypton or argon and fluorine. A fab uses it by the cylinder and cannot print without it.
why: Ukraine supplied about 70 percent of the world's neon before Russia invaded in 2022. Many chipmakers had added to their gas stockpiles after 2014, and several reported adequate supplies from China.

aka: wet chemical, wet processing, wet clean, cleaning chemicals, process chemicals
plain: Wet chemicals are the liquids a wafer is dipped in or sprayed with between steps: acids that strip a layer, solvents that remove resist, and ultrapure water rinses. Wet processing is any step done in liquid.
why: As of 2021 five firms held more than 60 percent of the wet chemicals market, and BIS controls wet processing tools by how selectively they etch one material over another.

aka: gallium, germanium, antimony
plain: Gallium and germanium are metals used in chips other than silicon logic, gallium in compound chips such as radio parts, LEDs and lasers, germanium in fiber optics, infrared optics and solar cells. Both are recovered as byproducts, gallium from processing bauxite and germanium from certain zinc ores and coal.
why: USGS put China's share of world production of primary low-purity gallium at 99 percent in February 2026, and China has required licenses to export both metals since August 2023. Its December 2024 ban on exports of both to the United States is suspended until 27 November 2026.

aka: rare earth, rare-earth, rare earth elements, medium and heavy rare earths
plain: The rare earths are a group of metals, including samarium and yttrium, that go into the strong magnets in motors, disk drives and wind turbines, and into some lasers and glass.
why: Beijing put seven of them under export license in April 2025, and in October 2025 claimed jurisdiction over foreign goods containing Chinese rare earths worth 0.1 percent or more of their value, a rule now suspended until 10 November 2026.

aka: metal-oxide resists, metal oxide resist, tin-oxide resist, metal-oxide EUV photoresist
plain: A metal-oxide resist is a photoresist built on clusters with a tin-oxide core. It absorbs more extreme ultraviolet light than a chemically amplified resist, which matters because an EUV dose arrives as relatively few photons.
why: Resist makers aim it at High-NA tools and the tightest pitches. JSR agreed in 2021 to buy Inpria, an Oregon maker of these resists, and a vehicle of a Japanese state-backed fund took 84.36 percent of JSR in 2024.

aka: HPC, HPC platform, high-performance computers
plain: High-performance computing is the industry's name for the heavy end of the market: supercomputers, AI accelerators and the server processors beside them. A foundry's HPC platform is the version of a node tuned for those chips.
why: AI accelerators belong to this segment and push its demands further. Ajinomoto counts 22 layers of its film in a 2026 AI package substrate, against 18 on a high-performance computing substrate around 2023.

aka: chips, microchip, microchips, semiconductor chip
plain: A chip is a small rectangle of silicon, usually smaller than a fingernail, that carries a complete electronic circuit made of billions of transistors. It is cut from a wafer after the circuit has been built up on it layer by layer.
why: Everything on the site is about how these rectangles get made, and who can stop the making.

aka: MR-MUF, Advanced MR-MUF, TC-NCF bonding
plain: Two ways of joining the thinned memory chips in an HBM stack. In TC-NCF, thermocompression with non-conductive film, each chip is pressed onto the one below under heat with a thin insulating film between them, and Samsung uses it for its twelve-high HBM3E. In MR-MUF, used by SK hynix, the chips are stacked first, and a liquid protective material is injected between them and hardened.
why: Thinner chips and taller stacks warp more easily, and both methods aim to control that. SK hynix says its Advanced MR-MUF also dissipates heat well.
